manifest.title: Forward Deployed Engineer
manifest.summary: Modules and a staged capstone on the work that sits between a customer’s messy problem and a system that survives contact with it: scoping, integration, bounded AI, evaluation, security, deployment, operations and handoff. It assumes you can already build software, and it grades the judgement rather than the syntax.
outcomes: Turn an ambiguous customer request into a scope with a baseline, a measurable success condition and stated non-goals.
Integrate a real-shaped external system: dirty records, pagination, throttling, duplicate delivery and identity boundaries.
Decide where deterministic code is the right answer and where a model earns its place, then bound what the model is allowed to do.
Evaluate a solution against a held-out set, separating retrieval failure from generation failure and quality from cost and latency.
Deploy into a cloud account the customer owns, and refuse a rollout the health, configuration and migration evidence has not cleared.
Handle a rollout, an incident and a handoff without inventing certainty you do not have.
nonGoals: A certification. Finishing produces a record of what you passed in these exercises, nothing more.
Evidence of production experience or any claim about employment. Completion says what you did here.
A vendor course. No provider account, paid API or specific framework is required, and none is taught as the answer.
Server-verified Python execution. Python appears as reading practice; anything you run locally is self-reviewed.
A prompt-engineering course. Prompt wording alone never passes a security or evaluation exercise here.
manifest.entryRequirement: You should be comfortable building and shipping software in at least one of the Fullstack, Frontend or Backend tracks: HTTP, a database or an API you have integrated, and JavaScript or TypeScript you can debug. The optional diagnostic measures the rest and recommends bridges; it never blocks anything and grants no exemption on its own.

activities.title: Two worked decompositions
activities.summary: Follow the dashboard and employee-sync cases from uncertainty to a bounded test and a changed constraint.

activities.title: The dashboard nobody trusts
activities.summary: Trace disputed shipment totals without writing to either source.
activities.scenario: A fictional operations desk uses a dashboard to choose which late shipments to investigate. Its totals differ from the billing export. The sponsor asks for a new dashboard in two weeks; the operator still compares CSV files by hand. You have read-only access to both sources and can observe one morning shift. No source has been declared authoritative for shipment status.

activities.title: Synchronise two employee systems
activities.summary: Define field ownership and ordering before synchronising employee records.
activities.scenario: A fictional company keeps payroll details in one service and office access in another. Names and email addresses can change; both systems expose an immutable employee identifier. Payroll owns employment status, Facilities owns badge groups. The requested pilot covers twenty employees, runs nightly and must not grant access to a person whose employment has ended.

activities.title: Two weeks or two months
activities.summary: Negotiate a useful delivery within a fixed deadline and access boundary.
activities.scenario: A fictional support team asks for ticket classification, knowledge search, automatic replies and reporting. A review with operators identifies classification as their largest repetitive task. The sponsor needs usable evidence in two weeks; a full integration is estimated at two months. Existing policy requires a person to approve customer messages. The pilot can read one ticket queue but cannot send messages.

activities.title: The requested feature conflicts with the workflow
activities.summary: Check the operator’s decision before accepting a requested feature.
activities.scenario: A fictional account team asks for automatic approval of refund requests. Observation shows that most time goes into finding the purchase and checking an existing eligibility policy. The finance owner requires a person to approve each payment. You may prototype a read-only purchase lookup and eligibility summary, but you cannot change the approval policy.

activities.title: Intermittent production API timeouts
activities.summary: Resolve uncertain side effects without treating timeouts as proof of failure.
activities.scenario: A fictional integration times out on roughly one request in a hundred. Operators report that large exports are affected more often. The customer asks for a database rewrite. You have request ids, latency traces and a read-only log sample; the external API has a documented rate limit. Retrying a write can create duplicate jobs unless its idempotency key is reused.

activities.title: A regulated customer considers model hosting
activities.summary: Compare a hosting plan against workload and operating constraints.
activities.scenario: A fictional customer’s written data policy permits sensitive document processing only in an approved private network. No hosted model endpoint is approved yet. The customer has a small platform team and an eight-week pilot window. A deterministic rules baseline solves a narrow subset of requests. You must compare options without treating a hosting label as evidence of security.

activities.title: Duplicate invoice events
activities.summary: Reconcile an uncertain payment and prevent a duplicate external effect.
activities.scenario: A fictional accounts team receives payment events from a provider. Delivery is at least once; each event has a stable event id and each invoice has its own id. The team wants an internal settlement workflow. A timeout can occur after the provider commits a payment. The pilot must never pay an invoice twice and may keep a reconciliation queue for uncertain outcomes.

activities.title: Answers from a private knowledge base
activities.summary: Bound evidence-backed answers by source access and freshness.
activities.scenario: A fictional support desk wants faster answers from a knowledge base. Documents have tenant access rules and revision dates; some articles are superseded. The pilot uses fixed retrieval results and authored model responses, not a live model. Every suggested answer must cite an accessible current source, or abstain for human review.

activities.title: The pilot is fast but unused
activities.summary: Measure an operational outcome and plan for adoption.
activities.scenario: A fictional operations pilot passes its offline checks and reduces a demonstrated lookup from ninety seconds to ten. Two weeks later, operators rarely open it. They explain that it lives outside their main ticket tool and loses their current ticket context. The sponsor asks for a larger model. You can modify a browser link and a read-only lookup, but not the ticket vendor’s core interface.

activities.title: A tenfold traffic spike
activities.summary: Plan burst traffic around a shared downstream request budget.
activities.scenario: A fictional service handles fifty jobs a minute under a two-minute completion objective. A launch may send five hundred jobs a minute. The downstream API accepts at most one hundred requests a minute; some jobs are urgent and others may wait. Repeating an accepted job must not repeat its customer notification. The sponsor asks to scale every worker tenfold.

activities.title: Two warehouses with intermittent connectivity
activities.summary: Keep disconnected reservations honest about shared-stock authority.
activities.scenario: A fictional inventory pilot spans two warehouses. Scanners can be offline for an hour. Each scan has a device-generated operation id; the same operation can upload again after reconnection. The central inventory service owns available-to-sell quantities. The customer asks both sites to promise stock immediately even while offline.

activities.title: Turn repeated custom work into a product proposal
activities.summary: Separate reusable mechanics from customer-specific boundaries.
activities.scenario: A fictional delivery team has integrated three customers’ ticket exports. Each adapter repeats pagination, tenant-scoped configuration and field validation, while the customers use different status vocabularies and retention policies. Product has one planning slot next month. The sponsor wants to copy the most recent customer’s adapter for everyone.

levels.missing: Restates the request without identifying who does the work today or what it costs them.
levels.partial: Names the operator and the pain, but has no measurable baseline and no stated exclusion.
levels.adequate: Identifies the operator, the current pain, a measurable baseline, what is out of scope, and the condition that would count as success.
levels.strong: As adequate, plus a tradeoff argued rather than asserted, and a coherent response when a requirement changes.

levels.missing: The described approach cannot work as specified.
levels.partial: Works on the happy path; a named failure mode in the brief is unhandled.
levels.adequate: Handles every failure mode the brief names, with the behaviour on each stated.
levels.strong: As adequate, plus a failure mode the brief did not name, found from the fixtures.

levels.partial: Handles missing fields, but not duplicates, pagination or repeated delivery.
levels.adequate: Handles missing fields, duplicates, pagination, throttling and repeated delivery, and says what it does with a record it cannot use.
levels.strong: As adequate, and the reconciliation is idempotent under replay in either order.

levels.missing: No measurement, or a demo presented as evidence.
levels.partial: A single aggregate number over cases the design was built against.
levels.adequate: A held-out set, a baseline to compare against, and quality reported separately from cost and latency.
levels.strong: As adequate, plus a slice where the average hides a failure, and an abstention rate reported alongside accuracy.

levels.missing: Retrieved or generated content is treated as trusted input.
levels.partial: Injection is mentioned, but a tool call can still act on unverified content.
levels.adequate: Untrusted content cannot authorize an action, cross a tenant boundary or widen a permission, and the check is in code rather than in wording.
levels.strong: As adequate, plus an adversarial case the brief did not supply, and a stated blast radius for the worst outcome.

levels.missing: No signal to watch and no way back.
levels.partial: Logs, but nothing that would show the failure before a customer does.
levels.adequate: A signal that would catch the named failure, a rollback that is safe to run, and an owner for the service.
levels.strong: As adequate, plus what the rollback cannot undo, and how the state left behind is reconciled.

levels.missing: The reader cannot tell what was decided or why.
levels.partial: Decisions are listed; the reasoning behind them is not.
levels.adequate: Decisions, the reason for each, the open questions, and what the reader has to do next.
levels.strong: As adequate, written for a named audience, with uncertainty stated rather than smoothed over.
